title: Steeple Sites: Church Land for Satellite Ground Stations
angle: Pairing 2: Space economy x Weird/niche/overlooked markets (hobbies, collectibles, faith, subcultures)
one_liner: Master-lease deals with denominations to host satellite ground stations, gateways and RF sensors on steeples and surplus church land, sold to operators as a ready-made site portfolio.
customer: Ground-station-as-a-service networks, smallsat IoT and EO operators, and direct-to-cell or broadband constellation operators needing gateways. Congregations and dioceses are paid as hosts.
problem: Launch has flooded orbit (321 launches, 4,517 satellites deployed in 2025, about 10,400 Starlinks), and carrier partnerships are multiplying, so downlink capacity, gateways and RF-quiet sites are a constraint. Site acquisition is slow, one farm or roof at a time. Meanwhile congregations own tall, zoning-friendly structures and acreage, monthly attendance is stuck at about 33%, and many boards need rental income or surplus-property solutions.
solution: Negotiate master-lease templates with denominational property boards (diocesan or conference trustees). Pre-screen sites for line of sight, RF noise, power, fiber and zoning, and package them into portfolios by latitude and orbit. Partner integrators handle permitting and install, and congregations get a share.
why_now: The spectrum land-grab settled (EchoStar's $23B sale to AT&T closed in July 2026, and the $17B sale to SpaceX), MNO satellite deals are multiplying, and every country-level service needs terrestrial infrastructure. Congregation attendance has plateaued at a low level, so property decisions are live.
revenue_model: A $5-15k site-acquisition fee per signed site paid by the operator, 15-20% of lease revenue for the life of the lease, and install margin. Congregations target $6-24k per year (to be validated).
non_obvious_insight: The tower industry already proved steeples are leasable, tall, permitted and governed by a few trustees, but satellite site teams chase farmland. One denomination negotiation can unlock hundreds of sites, and a closing parish is a seller with time pressure.
first_30_days: Pick one diocese or conference with rural clusters and pitch a pro-bono pilot lease template. Screen 30 sites from imagery, and approach 3 ground-network or IoT operators with a shortlist for a country where they lack coverage. Charge a $2-5k site-survey fee for a 10-site report as the first revenue.

title: Customs Broker-as-Software for LatAm Micro-Importers
one_liner: Tariff walls turn Temu-era resellers into importers, so sell them classification, duty prepayment and pre-filed declarations.
customer: Parcel consolidators and micro-importers in Mexico and Argentina, and courier forwarders serving them.
problem: Temu has 105M LatAm monthly users, Mexico charges 33.5% on parcels and Argentina proposes a 30% duty. Resellers now face classification, valuation and tax questions, and brokers charge per-entry fees that kill small shipments.
solution: An HS-code classifier, duty calculator, pre-filed declaration flow and duty prepayment float. The wedge is consolidators shipping 200-1,000 parcels a week from China.
why_now: Anti-parcel walls went up across LatAm in 2025-26, and Indonesia's de minimis cut shows the pattern spreading.
revenue_model: $2-5 per parcel plus 1-2% on duty financing.
non_obvious_insight: Tariff walls do not kill cross-border demand, they create a compliance tax, and the seller of compliance wins on volume.
first_30_days: Partner with two forwarders and cover the 20 most common HS codes for their volume.

title: Hours Wallet for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-first tool that proves 80 hours or $580 a month of work for gig and cash earners, paid by Medicaid plans and clinics that lose money when members drop off.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans, FQHCs and hospital financial-counseling teams paying per enrolled or retained member. Users: adults 19-64 in the Medicaid expansion group with irregular income (gig, seasonal, cash, self-employed).
problem: The CMS interim final rule (June 1, 2026) requires about 43 states plus DC to enforce 80 hours per month of work, service or school, or at least $580 per month of earnings, by January 1, 2027, at application and renewal. If compliance cannot be verified the person gets only 30 calendar days to prove it. Proof means pay stubs and letters from employers or volunteer organizations. Arkansas's 2018 requirement cost 18,000 people coverage for failing to meet work or reporting rules.
solution: SMS or WhatsApp-first app that (a) connects gig-platform exports or bank deposits to test the $580 income alternative, (b) sends one-tap timestamped attestation links to a boss, food-bank coordinator or volunteer supervisor, (c) auto-formats the state's monthly report and files it, (d) alerts the member before the 30-day cure window closes, and (e) screens for exemptions such as parents or caretakers of children under 14 and disability. It gives the payer a dashboard of at-risk members.
why_now: The federal rule is final as of June 2026 and states must be live by January 1, 2027 (some earlier, with Nebraska reportedly starting May 1, 2026). Self-attestation is only allowed for 2027, after which documentation is required, so 2027 is the last cheap window to build a member base and data habit before documentation hardens.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month or success fee per retained member from MCOs and FQHCs (about $3-$10/member/month or a bounty per successful renewal), with a free tier for members; secondary revenue from employer-attestation seats for staffing and home-care agencies.
non_obvious_insight: States must first use payroll and other data to verify compliance, which leaves the residual, hardest population (cash, gig and self-employed workers) exactly where a proof tool is needed. Payers, not members, have the money, because each lost member is lost capitation revenue. The CMS rule text (https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/medicaid-community-engagement-requirement-certain-individuals-interim-final-rule-comment-period-cms) gives the $580 alternative, 30-day cure period and exemptions, and KFF's data brief cites the 18,000 Arkansas coverage losses (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/issue-brief/understanding-the-intersection-of-medicaid-and-work-what-does-the-data-say/). Reddit was unreachable, so the r/personalfinance and r/legaladvice 'how do I prove my hours?' demand is forecast from the rule and explainers rather than quoted threads.
first_30_days: Build the $580 income test and attestation-link flow for Nebraska (reportedly already live) plus one January 2027 state. Approach 2 FQHCs and one regional MCO or hospital financial counseling team for a free pilot, and give the tool free to food banks and legal-aid groups as distribution. Aim for 200 pilot members, then convert the clinics to a per-member fee with retained-coverage data as the proof.

title: Instant Will-Serve Letters From Hydraulic Models
one_liner: Turn a utility's calibrated hydraulic model into a self-serve 'can you serve this address?' oracle that issues fire-flow and will-serve determinations in 48 hours instead of 4 weeks. It starts with developers and sprinkler designers and grows into a water-readiness index for data center and fab site selectors.
customer: Small and mid-size water utilities and the consulting engineering firms that maintain their models are the sellers. The payers are housing developers and fire sprinkler design firms ($250-2,000 per request), then data center, fab and beverage-plant site selection teams ($20-100k per year for the readiness data).
problem: Every subdivision, sprinkler design and industrial hookup needs a will-serve or fire-flow letter. Utilities own a calibrated hydraulic model (WaterGEMS, InfoWater, EPANET), but one or two engineers, or an outside consultant billing $2-8k per run, can operate it. Requests queue for weeks and stall housing and economic development. Worse, the answer 'we have plenty of water' is meaningless. The binding limits are max-day and peak-hour pressure in one pressure zone, fire reserve storage, tank turnover and water age, and the wastewater plant's discharge limits. Big buyers don't know that, and many utilities can't answer within the time a site-selection process allows.
solution: Ingest the utility's model file (.inp or vendor formats) and pre-compute a grid of scenarios. For each node and pressure zone, calculate available fire flow at a 20 psi residual, the maximum added demand before minimum-pressure or velocity limits break, and the effect on tank cycling and water age. Wrap it in a web form and API: enter address, demand, fire-flow requirement, and get a preliminary letter with the utility's letterhead, assumptions and limits. Exceptions go to the utility's licensed engineer for review and stamp. Utilities set the fee and keep most of it. The large-load layer adds wastewater and pretreatment limits, reclaimed-water availability, drought stage and water-rights status. It is published as a 'water hookup readiness' score by utility, like the power-availability maps that data center developers already buy.
why_now: The data center build-out has made water availability a headline and a local permitting fight, and site selection teams already buy power-availability intelligence but have no water equivalent. Housing permitting reform is speeding the approvals that come before utility review, which makes the utility review the bottleneck. Open-source tooling (EPANET and Sandia's WNTR) plus LLM agents that can read model files and draft letters make productizing this feasible for a small team. Many utilities finished models under recent risk-and-resilience assessments and master plans, so the models exist and are unused.
revenue_model: Utility SaaS of $15-40k per year, or free in exchange for a revenue share on developer fees. Per-request fees of $250-2,000 paid by developers, with the utility keeping 50-70%. Data subscriptions of $20-100k per year to site selectors, land brokers and hyperscaler real-estate teams. A consulting-firm channel where the engineering firm resells to its 10-30 utility clients.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not water. It is the one person who is allowed to run the model. The calibrated model is the most valuable unused asset a utility owns, and the answer developers want is hydraulic (peak-day and fire-flow at one node), not a volume in an annual water permit.
first_30_days: Approach one consulting engineering firm that maintains models for 10 or more small utilities and pitch productizing its most repeated task. Build a thin front end on WNTR or EPANET and offer one utility a free pilot: a public fire-flow map plus a letter template. Run the first 20 requests semi-manually, with the engineer generating and signing outputs in the background. Charge local sprinkler design firms $250 per fire-flow letter. Use the results to show turnaround times to two more utilities and to start a data-center-readiness prototype for one region.

title: One Recert: Housing Paperwork Keeps Medicaid Coverage
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Real estate (office-to-resi, vacancy, property mgmt, affordability)
one_liner: Reuse the income and employment paperwork affordable-housing operators already collect every year to stop residents' Medicaid from lapsing under the new work requirements, paid per retained member by Medicaid health plans.
customer: Medicaid managed-care organizations in expansion states (pay per retained member-month or per completed redetermination), plus LIHTC/HUD affordable-housing owners (pay per unit for lower delinquency and turnover). Hospitals in expansion states are a third payer.
problem: Work requirements hit all 41 expansion states on Jan 1, 2027 (Nebraska has been live since May 1, 2026), with 5.5-6.3M projected coverage losses and a 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hit to hospitals. Losses are mostly paperwork failures rather than true ineligibility (Arkansas's 2018 experiment saw about 18,000 people drop off largely through reporting failures). Each lost member is lost capitation for the plan, unpaid bills for the hospital and, later, a late-rent risk for the landlord.
solution: With resident consent, ingest the annual and interim income/employment verifications that housing operators already gather. Map them to state rules (80 hours a month, or roughly $580 in monthly income, plus exemptions such as caregivers), build the compliance packet, submit it to the state portal or plan, and send monthly nudges when hours dip. A remote call team plus the property's resident-services coordinator handles the human steps.
why_now: The Jan 1, 2027 nationwide deadline is three months away and plans are setting 2027 retention budgets now. Nebraska is a live proving ground today. ACA subsidy expiry already added about 4.8M uninsured, so plans and hospitals are hunting for any lever that keeps members covered.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month retention fee or $75-150 per completed redetermination from plans; $2-4/unit/month SaaS from housing owners; hospital-funded pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Affordable-housing recertification is the most audit-grade employment and income record low-income adults have, and nobody reuses it. The housing operator is also the only party that sees the resident monthly and has its own reason to care, since Medicaid loss leads to medical debt and then late rent.
first_30_days: Start in Nebraska. Sign one affordable operator with 1,000-3,000 units and one Medicaid plan. Hand-build the packet workflow with forms and spreadsheets for 100 consenting residents, measure retention against a comparison group, and price the service per retained member. Clone state by state ahead of Jan 1.

title: Medicaid Work-Rule Retention Packets for Health Plans
one_liner: A pay-per-retained-member service that assembles the income-proxy, exemption and medical-frailty evidence packets Medicaid expansion enrollees need to keep coverage, sold to the health plans and clinics that lose revenue when members are dropped.
customer: Medicaid managed-care plans (especially regional and provider-sponsored plans in expansion states), FQHC networks, and hospital systems with large expansion panels. Secondary buyers: state agencies and counties that have said they will not add staff.
problem: Work requirements start January 1, 2027 in 44 states. CMS projects 2.3M people lose Medicaid in 2027, and 55% of enrollees are unaware of the rule. States are scraping existing data. Nebraska hired no new staff, and its medical-frailty code list omitted certain cancers, heart failure and HIV. North Carolina bars self-attestation and requires 3 months of records. About 25% of Dare County's expansion enrollees are self-employed. County Medicaid units have ~10% vacancy and staff with only 11-13 months' experience. A KFF-cited expert calls hours tracking 'a problem no state has solved at scale.'
solution: Consent-based enrollee flow, started via text or QR code at a clinic or from a plan's outreach. The enrollee links bank, gig-platform, payroll or 1099 data through open-banking and income-verification connectors. The system computes monthly income against the $580 threshold (80 hours x $7.25) that satisfies the rule, with seasonal averaging where the state allows. It then generates a state-formatted verification submission. In parallel it mines the plan's or clinic's claims and EHR history to match the medically frail categories and produces clinician attestation forms. It tracks the 30-day grace window and 6-month redeterminations. Volunteer-hour and school verification come from partner organizations. A human navigator queue handles exceptions.
why_now: CMS issued its interim final rule June 1, 2026 and a medical-frailty implementation deck on September 8. Nebraska (May 1) and Montana (July 1) are live, so real failure modes are visible. States may request extra information from enrollees in year one, and exemption self-attestation is allowed only once before 2028, so documentation becomes mandatory after that. The January deadline sets hard budget urgency.
revenue_model: Per-packet fee plus per-member-per-month retention fee paid by the plan or clinic. Assumption to validate: a retained expansion member is worth hundreds of dollars per month in capitation, so $30-100 per retained member is easily justified. Optional state contracts priced per verification.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is evidence for people the state cannot see in wage data (self-employed, gig, seasonal), not caseworker capacity. Health plans and clinics, not states, have both the financial incentive and the claims data to prove frailty. The federal income equivalent ($580/month) turns an impossible hours-tracking problem into a cash-flow calculation. Evidence: NC counties describe the informal-economy documentation gap, 10% vacancy, no self-attestation and 3 months of records (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Nebraska confirmed the ~$580 income option and said it will not hire or add staff (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-closer-look-at-nebraska-the-first-state-planning-to-implement-a-medicaid-work-requirement/), and its frailty code list had gaps (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/nebraska-medicaid-work-requirements-launch-first-state/818992/). CMS projects 2.3M coverage losses in 2027 (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/cms-medicaid-work-requirements-final-rule-state-guidance/821631/). State staffing gaps: https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/. Risk: 26 states are suing over the rule.
first_30_days: Offer free pilots to 1-2 FQHCs in Nebraska or Montana, where enrollees already face the requirement. Build on an open-banking connector and an income-verification API. Draft the income-proxy calculator and a frailty-evidence template from CMS's September deck. Book meetings with member-retention leads at 5 regional Medicaid plans, with a paid pilot targeted for the November-December pre-January enrollment wave. Get a HIPAA BAA and consent language in place first.

title: Licensed Principal-of-Record for Financial Agents
angle: Pairing 1: AI agents & agent economy x Finance
one_liner: Buy a retiring independent insurance agency, then rent its licenses, carrier appointments and supervision layer to AI-agent builders that need a legally accountable entity behind every quote and bind.
customer: Startups building consumer or SMB agents that quote, recommend or bind insurance (later, money-movement advice), plus independent agencies that want to deploy agents under compliance cover.
problem: An agent that solicits or binds coverage is doing a licensed activity, but software has no license. Fifty-state producer licensing and carrier appointments take years, so agent startups avoid the vertical, use lead-gen workarounds, or run unsupervised. Regulators are converging on the idea that a licensed entity must own what the AI says (the NAIC AI bulletin has been adopted by roughly two dozen states).
solution: Acquire one or two small independent agencies (about 1.5-2x revenue, seller-financed) and inherit their resident and non-resident licenses, appointments and renewal book. Onboard agent builders as sub-producers. Provide the supervision layer: conversation and decision logging, rule-based disclosure and suitability guardrails, escalation to a licensed human reviewer, E&O coverage and regulator-ready audit trails.
why_now: Independent agencies are shrinking (39k in 2024 to 37k in 2026), so owners are selling. About 95% of commercial insurance is still sold by humans. Q2 2026 insurtech funding hit $2.44B with 99.1% going to AI-centric firms (Outmarket raised $34.5M at a $335M valuation). ISO's generative-AI exclusion (CG 40 47) is pushing buyers to look for affirmative cover.
revenue_model: A 20-40% override on commissions from agent-originated policies, a monthly supervision and platform fee per agent-builder ($2-10k), and the acquired book's renewal commissions as base cash flow.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not the model but a clean license history plus carrier appointments, which a retiring agency owner will sell cheaply and whose renewal stream funds the company. Whoever becomes the accountable principal for autonomous sellers collects a toll on all of them, a US analog to the UK Appointed Representative regime.
first_30_days: Shortlist 5 agencies (owners 60+, $500k-$2M revenue, licensed in 10+ states) through perpetuation brokers and sign an LOI with seller financing on one. Sign 3 design partners (AI quoting or benefits-navigator startups) for shadow-mode onboarding. Get a written opinion from insurance-regulatory counsel on how AI-conducted solicitations are treated for sub-producers in the first 3 states.

title: Independent Battery Safety Review for Counties
one_liner: Sell counties and fire marshals a developer-funded third-party plan review, hazard analysis and first-responder plan for every battery project.
customer: Storage developers pay the fees, usually through a county-controlled escrow. Counties and fire authorities contract the reviewer, and insurers use the dossiers.
problem: US storage installs hit a record 18.9 GWh in Q2 2026. After the January 2025 Moss Landing fire, hearings turn hostile and local moratoria spread. Fire departments lack expertise, NFPA 855 and UL 9540A data are hard to interpret, and developers lose 6-12 months in permitting.
solution: An independent safety dossier: hazard mitigation analysis, interpretation of large-scale fire test data, an emergency response plan, a thermal and off-gas monitoring plan and training for local responders. Sell it as fixed-price packages with an annual inspection option, plus a model county ordinance and review checklist.
why_now: Record installs are moving into populated areas, moratoria and insurer repricing are active, and code cycles are updating.
revenue_model: $25-80k per project via the county escrow, $5-10k a year for inspections, and training contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is trust, not technology. A reviewer the county chooses but the developer pays, like a planning consultant, speeds approvals and removes the NIMBY veto.
first_30_days: Draft a model BESS review ordinance and checklist. Offer free reviews to three counties with pending applications. Get two developers to pay for pre-application dossiers. Retain a fire-protection PE and a retired fire marshal.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.

title: Independent Pharmacy GLP-1 Aftercare Studios
one_liner: A turnkey cash-pay aftercare membership that gives independent pharmacies their first PBM-free service line.
customer: Independent community pharmacies (~17k in the US). One report has ~41% not dispensing obesity GLP-1s in Q4 2025 over poor reimbursement.
problem: Insiders assume Walmart, CVS and Amazon win GLP-1 care because of scale. Independents get squeezed by PBM reimbursement below cost and skip the category, even though they see patients monthly and pharmacists can check dose, side effects and nutrition.
solution: A 'studio' kit: leased body-composition scale, a protocol (dose-step check, protein and strength plan, red-flag triage), scheduling and billing for a $39-59/month cash membership, and links to pill and vial cash-pay fulfillment. Includes collaborative-practice documents and, where state law allows pharmacist prescribing, protocols for it. Monthly outcomes report to the pharmacist and to referral partners.
why_now: $149-$299 cash pills remove the need for dispensing margin to justify the category. Lilly and Novo cash channels route through retail pharmacies. Big chains launched their own pharmacist support programs in 2026, so independents need a counter-offer.
revenue_model: $199-399/month SaaS per pharmacy plus 20% of membership revenue, plus device lease.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 is the first drug category where a pharmacy can earn from services with zero PBM exposure. Independent pharmacists are more trusted locally than a chain's app and have a natural monthly touchpoint.
first_30_days: Partner with one state pharmacy association or wholesaler buying group. Pilot in 5 pharmacies at $49/month. Track retention and a muscle proxy (grip and chair-stand) for the first cohort.

title: Widow-First Retention Drills for Wealth Advisors
one_liner: Sell independent advisors an annual 'if one of us dies' rehearsal for couples, because the defection risk sits at the first spouse's death, not with the kids.
customer: Independent RIAs and small wealth teams ($150M-$2B AUM) whose median client is 65+. The buyer is the firm principal or COO.
problem: The industry spends on next-gen events with heirs. Cerulli says about $54T of the transfer is spousal and about $40T of that goes to widowed women. The survivor is grieving, holds a house full of logins and unknown accounts, and has to decide whether to keep the advisor. Advisors are commonly said to lose most widows within a year (widely cited, verify). The cause is usually friction, not performance.
solution: A 90-minute 'Survivor Fire Drill' run by the advisor's team with a software kit. Each spouse's death is simulated in turn. The tool builds a First-90-Days playbook: who to call, which accounts exist, which autopays must keep running, and where the documents are. It audits titling and beneficiaries from the survivor's point of view and flags single points of failure, such as only one spouse knowing the passwords. It then schedules pre-agreed advisor check-ins at day 3, 14, 45 and 90. The advisor gets a dashboard of which couples have done the drill and where their exposure is.
why_now: Cerulli's Sept 2026 work frames retention of the transfer as the priority, and 89% of surveyed firms call family meetings essential. Wealth managers are buying heir-engagement tools, yet the first wave of money is spousal and the widow is under-served. Cheap document ingestion and secure vaults make the kit affordable for small firms.
revenue_model: $300-$700 per household per year billed to the firm, or a $25-40K/yr platform fee for a 100-household book. The ROI pitch: keeping one $1.5M widow at a 1% fee is worth $15K a year.
non_obvious_insight: The heir-retention narrative aims at the wrong person on the wrong day. Widows rarely leave over portfolio returns. They leave because nobody made the first 90 days easy. A rehearsal also works where estate planning fails, because people avoid 'planning' but will attend a scheduled drill.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 RIAs through advisor communities and podcasts. Run drills by hand with a spreadsheet and printed binder for each firm's 10 oldest couples. Record time-to-locate-accounts and the number of single-point-of-failure findings. Charge a $2.5K pilot fee and turn the findings into a retention case study the advisor can show prospects.

title: Off-Market Farmland Transfer Radar
one_liner: Score farm parcels likely to change hands through estates before they are ever listed.
customer: Farmland brokers, ag lenders, farmland REITs, land-buying farm groups and ag estate attorneys.
problem: Listing data shows only the visible market, but about a third of landlords are 75 or older, only about 1 in 4 farmers has a succession plan, and millions of acres will move through estates.
solution: Combine public probate filings, assessor and ownership records and landlord-age modeling into county-level parcel transfer scores and alerts, sold by subscription.
why_now: The 2026 reporting on the invisible farmland transfer and a multi-year farm-income squeeze mean lenders and buyers want early visibility into forced and estate sales.
revenue_model: County-pack subscriptions of $300-1,500/month, plus success fees to brokers and lenders on originated deals.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest land flow is invisible to listing-based data, and the underlying records are public but fragmented county by county. Data plumbing rather than model quality is the moat.
first_30_days: Scrape probate and assessor data in three Midwest counties, build a first transfer-likelihood score, and pitch 15 local brokers and two ag lenders on a paid pilot.

title: Independent Lab Certifying AI Detectors and Watermarks
one_liner: An AV-TEST-style lab that red-teams detectors and watermarks every month and sells certification seals and buyer reports.
customer: Detection and watermark vendors (seals and re-tests), and enterprise buyers such as platform trust-and-safety teams, publishers, insurers and law firms that need to know which tool to trust.
problem: Detection is crowded and cheap (Pangram $9M raise at $20/month, GPTZero $10M, GetReal $18M, Reality Defender $15M, Deezer licensing its detector) and buyers cannot verify accuracy claims. Pangram claims about 1 in 10,000 false positives, yet a reviewer still saw human sentences flagged. Watermark removers appeared within a week of Sora. Public 'human vs AI' scores now shape reputations, but no one audits them.
solution: A monthly adversarial benchmark across text, audio, image and video. It uses stratified known-human gold sets (for example non-native English writers and niche music genres), fresh output from current models, adaptive attacks (paraphrasers, re-encoding, watermark removers) and fixed false-positive operating points. Publish a leaderboard, and issue 'certified at or below X% false-positive rate on domain Y' seals and watermark robustness ratings.
why_now: Detectors are being embedded in reader-facing features (Substack, LinkedIn, Deezer licensing), EU Art. 50 pushes marking and detection into procurement checklists, and reputational stakes for false positives are visible.
revenue_model: $15-60k/year per vendor for testing and seals, $5-25k/year buyer subscriptions for detailed results, and $10-40k custom bake-offs.
non_obvious_insight: When the buyer cannot verify a product's core claim, the independent tester captures value, which is why UL, AV-TEST and NSS Labs exist. The scarce asset is a fresh, curated, known-human gold set plus an adversarial toolkit.
first_30_days: Publish a free benchmark v0 of six text detectors and three audio detectors in three weeks, using 2,000 volunteer-written human documents and fresh AI outputs. DM vendors and trust-and-safety leads with a paid 'verified retest' offer. First payers will be challengers who want a credible badge.

title: Toll Fermentation in Dead Alt-Protein Plants
one_liner: Buy or lease bankrupt alt-protein bioreactor capacity for pennies and run it as a toll fermenter for whey-alternative brands.
customer: Precision-fermentation whey and casein brands at Series A/B stage, plus protein buyers who need non-dairy supply.
problem: More than 70 alt-protein companies have merged or shut since Sept 2024, leaving idle fermentation assets, while whey is sold out and brands like Verley have product and FDA clearance but not plant capacity.
solution: Acquire or option distressed fermenters and downstream-processing lines, retool them into a multi-tenant toll plant, and sign take-or-pay reservations with whey-alternative brands.
why_now: H1 2026 alt-protein funding was only $197M (of which $132M fermentation), assets are cheap, and whey concentrate is up 108% in two years with buyers shifting from ESG goals to supply-risk mitigation.
revenue_model: Toll fee per kg processed plus take-or-pay capacity reservation fees; asset purchase is financed by anchor-tenant contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The sector's collapse is a capacity bargain arriving exactly when demand for non-dairy protein flipped from a values purchase to a supply-security purchase. The assets are worth more to a toll operator than to their bankrupt owners.
first_30_days: Catalogue stranded plants through bankruptcy brokers and lender sale lists, get LOIs from 2-3 whey-alternative brands for reserved capacity, and take a purchase or lease option on one plant contingent on an anchor contract.

title: Certified Refurb Phone Pipeline for Africa
one_liner: The memory crunch kills the cheap new phone, so the next wave of African users arrives on graded, warrantied used handsets.
customer: Independent phone retailers and mid-size distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana, and telco handset-financing programmes.
problem: Memory is 30-40% of a phone's bill of materials, IDC calls sub-Rs 9,000 phones possibly permanently uneconomical, and the GSMA $40 phone is only a pilot. About 960M Africans under coverage are still offline, and the used-phone market is full of blacklisted, dying-battery lemons.
solution: Buy bulk trade-in lots from the Gulf, EU and Japan and grade them in software (battery health, IMEI/blacklist check, Play certification). Ship with a 6-month warranty and sell to retailers on 30-day credit. The wedge is IMEI-clean, warrantied lots for a handful of retailers in one market such as Lagos.
why_now: 2026 AI-driven memory prices broke the sub-$60 new-phone tier, and LatAm shipments fell 10%. The GSMA is piloting a $40 phone precisely because the market cannot produce one.
revenue_model: Roughly $8-15 gross margin per handset, plus warranty fees and a financing spread.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders wait for cheap new phones. The scarce asset is trust in used devices, and whoever certifies them owns the affordable tier once new supply disappears.
first_30_days: Source about 500 units from a Dubai or European refurbisher, grade them and place them with five retailers on consignment. Track return rates, which become the pricing moat.

title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.

title: Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data
one_liner: An audit that tells research buyers what share of their online-panel responses came from bots, agents or fraud farms, and recalibrates the study against a verified-human control sample.
customer: Insights heads at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms, UX-research teams, academic labs and pollsters who buy panel sample from third-party vendors at $5-500 per complete.
problem: One prompt to a commercial AI agent now passes screeners and attention checks. A controlled evaluation found synthetic respondents passing 99.8% of 6,000 attention-check trials. As little as 3-7% contaminated responses can invalidate conclusions. Panel vendors both sell the sample and score its quality, so buyers cannot trust the referee.
solution: A per-study data-quality audit. Response files (timings, paradata, device data, open-ends) go through a detection ensemble plus honeypot items. A subset of the same questionnaire goes to a small address-recruited, device-attested human panel as a ground-truth control. Deliver an audit stamp, contamination-adjusted estimates, and a vendor scorecard across suppliers.
why_now: Survey-fraud research in 2025-26 shows agents beating attention checks. An MIT-run $50K challenge is testing detection, and NORC published a fraud literature review. Election-season polling and pharma sample budgets raise the stakes, and buyers are asking who audits the panels.
revenue_model: $3-15k per study audit, $50-150k per year programmes for insights teams that spend $2-10M on sample, and vendor-scorecard subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Most anti-fraud tooling is sold by panel sellers, whose incentive is to under-report fraud. The scarce asset is not detection code but an independent, verified-human comparison group, because you cannot prove what is fake without a known-real reference.
first_30_days: Recruit about 2,000 verified humans by address-based mail or a university survey-centre partnership. Buy sample from six panel vendors yourself and publish a 'state of sample quality' benchmark. Offer free audits to five insights leaders who have posted about bad data.

title: CRA Continuity Kit for One-Person Vendors
one_liner: An outsourced EU Cyber Resilience Act desk that handles the 24h/72h/14-day vulnerability reporting clock and keeps a signed 10-year release vault with a dead-man's-switch escrow, built for micro-vendors with no security team.
customer: Solo and micro hardware, firmware, app and SaaS vendors that sell into the EU, such as ESP32 and Raspberry Pi based device makers on Tindie or Crowd Supply, small GmbHs, and indie app publishers. There is no size exemption. They pay EUR 79-399/month per product.
problem: CRA Article 14 reporting began 11 September 2026: a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour notification and a 14-day final report via ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. A one-person German GmbH selling firmware asks how to comply given CE marking, a technical file, 'every security update you ship has to stay available for 10 years' and no size threshold. Maintainers are already bailing out: the croniter fork was archived citing the CRA.
solution: A subscription that provides (1) a named on-call reporting desk that prepares and files the early warning, notification and final report on the vendor's delegated authority against a pre-agreed playbook; (2) SBOM generation and continuous vulnerability watch tied to the customer's release artifacts, to detect an 'actively exploited' trigger; (3) an immutable, signed release vault holding every shipped update for 10+ years, with a dead-man's-switch: if the vendor stops responding or dissolves, the firmware source and update artifacts are released to customers or a nominated steward; (4) a fixed-price 'CRA readiness sprint' that produces the technical-file skeleton and declaration-of-conformity scaffolding.
why_now: The reporting obligation went live 11 September 2026, so this is a forced-spend deadline, not a forecast. Full obligations follow in December 2027. Legal commentators say many still associate the CRA only with consumer IoT and are unprepared.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500 fixed-price readiness sprint, then EUR 79-399/month per product for the reporting retainer and vault, tiered by product count and risk class. Optional per-incident filing fee. Channel deals with device marketplaces and Linux/embedded distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not compliance dashboards (the Ask HN thread already lists Vulert, ReARM and the ORC WG hub) but staffed responsiveness and durable custody: a solo founder cannot staff a 24-hour clock or credibly promise 10 years of availability. A dead-man's-switch vault turns the founder's bus-factor into a compliance asset. Escrow at end of life is a recurring HN demand, e.g. 'When you release a product, you should be required to put the source code in escrow, so it can be released at EoL' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44531176, and vendors ask for escrow tooling https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46402528. Evidence of demand: one-person GmbH asking for help https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49520688; obligations and fines https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/11/eus-cyber-resilience-act-starts-the-24-hour-vulnerability-clock/5295821; croniter archived https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43168860.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 design partners from the Open Regulatory Compliance WG CRA hub, Torizon CRA summit attendees, and Tindie/Crowd Supply sellers, plus the author of the Ask HN thread. Sell the EUR 1,500 sprint with a written 24h playbook and SBOM pipeline for their repos. Stand up the vault on object-lock storage with signed manifests and a heartbeat check-in. Have a CRA-literate lawyer review the delegation-of-filing template. Convert sprint customers to the retainer.

title: Battery passport starter that feeds on repair-shop events
one_liner: A cheap battery-passport package for e-bike and small pack makers, plus a repair-shop scanning app that supplies the lifecycle events the passport is legally supposed to track.
customer: Small and mid-size European e-bike, e-scooter and cargo-bike brands, pack assemblers, and industrial or storage battery integrators above 2 kWh. The battery passport must exist from 18 Feb 2027. Independent repair shops and refurbishers are the second user group.
problem: From 18 Feb 2027, LMT, EV and industrial batteries over 2 kWh need a passport reachable by QR code and linked to a unique identifier. The Annex XIII list has 71 entries, but 'not every field is due in February 2027': fields are day-one, modelled-now-populated-later, or waiting on secondary legislation. Access-rights rules are slipping to Q4 2026 and key standards are still in draft. Passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes after repurposing or remanufacturing. As one guide says, 'a once-published PDF or marketing microsite is not enough'. Enterprise passport platforms are priced for large firms with compliance teams.
solution: Two products. (1) A brand starter package: a field-status mapper that says which of the 71 fields are due now, later or pending; ISO/IEC 15459-style unique ID and QR generation; a hosted passport page; and a written-authorisation template so the brand can legally delegate passport management to us. (2) A free repair-shop and refurbisher app that scans the QR, logs state-of-health tests, cell swaps, cycle data and second-life events, and pushes them into the brand's passport. Shops get a free workflow tool and repair leads. Brands pay for the passport and the event stream. This also lines up with the replaceable-battery rule that applies from 18 Feb 2027 and with the Right to Repair Directive.
why_now: The passport deadline is under 5 months away and the access-rights implementing act is late. Replaceable portable batteries and e-bike batteries become an obligation on the same date. Eighteen Member States had not notified full transposition of the Right to Repair Directive by September 2026, which leaves national repair rules unsettled while shops still have to service batteries.
revenue_model: Brand setup of EUR 2-5k. Subscription of roughly EUR 1-3 per battery per year (or a EUR 300-1,500 per month floor). Optional per-event fee for verified state-of-health tests. Later, a paid API for insurers and second-life buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells 'publish a QR page'. The law's real burden is a lifecycle record kept consistent across systems and updated when the battery is serviced or repurposed, and that happens in repair shops that no passport vendor serves. Evidence: 'The hard part is not publishing a page. The hard part is keeping model-level, plant-level, and individual-battery records consistent', passports must track state of health, cycle counts and status changes, and batteries allow the operator to authorise another actor in writing to manage the passport (https://infodpp.eu/en/blog/battery-dpp-deadline-february-2027/). Mid-scale companies are named as the likely pressure point (https://www.batterytechonline.com/design-manufacturing/preparing-for-eu-battery-qr-code-standards-in-2027) and passport software is described as badly priced for small manufacturers (https://dpp-tool.com/en/guide/dpp-software-comparison/). Replaceability and spare-battery availability from 18 Feb 2027 are covered at https://www.intertek.com/blog/2025/06-27-2027-reqs-for-removability-and-replaceability-of-batteries-in-electrical-products/. Right to Repair transposition gap: https://www.eunews.it/en/2026/09/25/right-to-repair-italy-and-17-other-countries-have-failed-to-transpose-the-directive-eu-infringement-proceedings-begin/.
first_30_days: Build a spreadsheet-based field-status mapper for the 71 fields and offer it as a free download. Contact 30 small e-bike brands and pack assemblers found through European trade fairs, cycling industry associations and importer lists. Sell 3 paid 'passport readiness sprint' engagements at EUR 1.5-3k each that end with a hosted pilot passport for one battery model. In parallel, recruit 10 independent e-bike shops to test the scan-and-log app on real service jobs.

title: Outfall Guardian for Data-Center Construction Sites
one_liner: Continuous outfall monitoring, rapid pathogen testing and auto-generated permit paperwork for contractors building data-center campuses and fabs.
customer: General contractors, owner's representatives and developers building $1B+ data-center and semiconductor campuses. Multi-million-dollar schedule risk gives them a real budget, and the contractor or owner pays.
problem: Cheyenne revoked Meta's discharge permit after a rare bacterium in its wastewater was traced to a construction site, and Ohio scrapped a general permit after more than 7,000 comments. Water quality, not just quantity, is now a siting risk. Contractors treat water as volume and have no biology or continuous-monitoring capability during dewatering, stormwater and hydrostatic testing.
solution: Off-the-shelf multiparameter sensors (turbidity, pH, conductivity, temperature) at each outfall, weekly rapid qPCR pathogen and bacterial testing through a partner lab, automated discharge-monitoring reports and a time-stamped 'permit defense file' that shows compliance before regulators ask. Add a community-facing dashboard.
why_now: Moratoria, permit revocations and public comment fights make regulators and neighbors ask for data. Capex on campuses has exploded, and delay costs are large.
revenue_model: $3-8k/site/month plus per-test lab fees and onboarding fees.
non_obvious_insight: The construction phase is the unmonitored weak link in a water-quality chain everyone else audits. Third-party telemetry works like insurance-grade evidence, and the buyer's motive is schedule protection, not sustainability.
first_30_days: Publish an analysis of the Cheyenne case as top-of-funnel. Contact 10 contractors and owner's reps active in Northern Virginia, Ohio, Texas, Wyoming and Arizona. Pilot at one site with commercial sensors and a contract lab, and offer the first month free in exchange for a case study.
